Notice of Pre-AIA  or AIA  Status
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA .
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(b):
(b)  CONCLUSION.—The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), second paragraph:
The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.
Claims 5 and 6 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor (or for applications subject to pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, the applicant), regards as the invention.
Claim 5 recites the limitation the index in line 1.  There is insufficient antecedent basis for this limitation in the claim.
Claim 6 properly depends on claim 5 and is therefore likewise rejected.
Examiner Remarks
Examiner interprets “the index” of claim 5 to be “the strength level” as claimed in claim 3 in examining the subject matter of claim 5.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102
In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis (i.e., changing from AIA  to pre-AIA ) for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
The following is a quotation of the appropriate paragraphs of 35 U.S.C. 102 that form the basis for the rejections under this section made in this Office action:
A person shall be entitled to a patent unless –
(a)(2) the claimed invention was described in a patent issued under section 151, or in an application for patent published or deemed published under section 122(b), in which the patent or application, as the case may be, names another inventor and was effectively filed before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
Claim(s) 1 – 5, 7, 8, 10, 12 – 16, 18, 19, 21, and 23 is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) as being anticipated by Du et al. (US 2021/0266604) (hereinafter Du).
Regarding claims 1, 12, and 23, Du teaches a video decoding method, a video decoding apparatus comprising a memory configured to store instructions and one or more processors configured to execute the instructions to cause the apparatus to perform the video decoding method (e.g. par. 238: describing that the video decoder includes memory storing instructions and one or more processors configured to execute the instructions), and a non-transitory computer readable medium that stores a set of instructions that is executable by one or more processors of an apparatus to cause the apparatus to perform the video decoding method (e.g. par. 238: describing a non-transitory computer readable medium storing instructions executable by one or more processors), the video decoding method comprising:
determining a direction of a reconstructed luma block (e.g. Figs. 21 and 24, and pars. 175 – 178, 191, and 224: depicting and describing that the system performs constraint directional enhancement filtering (CDEF) of a reconstructed luma (Y) block, performing CDEF including determining a direction of the luma block);
decoding an encoded bit stream to determine a plurality of filter coefficients associated with a directional cross component filter (e.g. pars. 175 and 217: describing that filtering strengths and weighting factors are obtained from the encoded bitstream, wherein filtering strengths and weighting factors are the equivalent of filter coefficients); and
applying the plurality of filter coefficients to the reconstructed luma block to determine an offset to the direction of the reconstructed luma block (e.g. par. 198: describing that the system applies the filter to the reconstructed luma block to determine an offset to the CDEF reconstructed luma block, wherein CDEF reconstructed luma block is the equivalent of the direction of the reconstructed luma block).
Turning to claims 2 and 13, Du teaches all of the limitations of claims 1 and 12, respectively, as discussed above. Du further teaches:
adding the offset to a reconstructed chroma block associated with the reconstructed luma block (e.g. Figs. 21 and 24, and pars. 191 and 198: depicting and describing that the offset is added to a reconstructed chroma block associated with the reconstructed luma block).
Regarding claims 3 and 14, Du teaches all of the limitations of claims 1 and 2, and claims 12 and 13, respectively, as discussed above. Du further teaches:
wherein adding the offset to the reconstructed chroma block comprises: decoding the encoded bit stream to determine a strength level associated with the offset; and adding the offset to the reconstructed chroma block at the strength level (e.g. pars. 193 and 217: describing that the system determines a weight associated with the offset from the bitstream and adds the offset to the reconstructed chroma block based on the determined weight, wherein the weight is the equivalent of the strength level).
Turning to claims 4 and 15, Du teaches all of the limitations of claims 1 - 3 , and claims 12 - 14, respectively, as discussed above. Du further teaches:
wherein the strength level is a positive integer (e.g. par. 217: describing that the weight is greater than zero, reasonably suggesting that the strength level is positive).
Regarding claims 5 and 16, Du teaches all of the limitations of claims 1 - 3 , and claims 12 - 14, respectively, as discussed above. Du further teaches:
wherein the index is signaled in coding parameters for a filter block (e.g. par. 217: describing that the offset weight is signaled in the coding parameters for the filtering block).
Turning to claims 7 and 18, Du teaches all of the limitations of claims 1 and 12, respectively, as discussed above. Du further teaches:
wherein the offset is determined: in parallel to a loop restoration unit, in parallel to a constraint directional enhancement filter, after the loop restoration unit is applied to the reconstructed luma block, or after the constraint directional enhancement filter is applied to the reconstructed luma block (e.g. Figs. 24 and 25, and pars. 206, 207, and 224: describing that the offset is determined in parallel to or after a loop restoration unit or in parallel to or after a constraint directional enhancement filter).
Regarding claims 8 and 19, Du teaches all of the limitations of claims 1 and 12, respectively, as discussed above. Du further teaches:
determining, based on a flag, whether the directional cross component filter is enabled for a video sequence or a video frame (e.g. par. 216: describing that the system determines, based on an enable flag, whether joint component filter is enabled for a video sequence (enabling flag signaled in the sequence parameter set) or a video frame (picture parameter set).
Turning to claims 10 and 21, Du teaches all of the limitations of claims 1 and 8, and claims 12 and 21, respectively, as discussed above. Du further teaches:
wherein the flag is signaled in a video sequence header or a video frame header (e.g. par. 216: describing that the JCF filter flag is signaled in the sequence parameter set or the picture parameter set, wherein the sequence parameter set is the equivalent of the video sequence header, and wherein the picture parameter set is the equivalent of the video frame header).
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
The text of those sections of Title 35, U.S. Code not included in this action can be found in a prior Office action.
The factual inquiries for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
Claim(s) 6 and 17  is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Du et al. (US 2021/0266604) (hereinafter Du) as applied to claims 5 and 16, respectively, above, and further in view of Chen et al., “An Overview of core coding Tools in the AV1 Video Codec,” 2018 Picture Coding Symposium (PCS), San Francisco, CA, 2018, pp. 41 – 45 (hereinafter Chen), as cited by applicant.
Regarding claims 6 and 17, Du teaches all of the limitations of claims 1-3 and 5, and claims 12 -14 and 16, respectively, as discussed above. Du does not explicitly teach:
wherein the filter block is a 64x64 block.
Chen, however, teaches a video decoding method and apparatus:
wherein the filter block is a 64x64 block (e.g. section 4: describing that the filter block is a 64x64 block).
It therefore would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to modify the teachings of Du by adding the teachings of Chen in order for the filter block to be a 64x64 block. One of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to make such a modification because the modification improves coding efficiency.
Claim(s) 9 and 20 is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Du et al. (US 2021/0266604) (hereinafter Du) as applied to claims 8 and 19, resepctively above, and further in view of Hu et al. (US 2021/0368169)(hereinafter Hu).
Regarding claims 9 and 20, Du teaches all of the limitations of claims 1 and 8, and claims 12 and 19, respectively, as discussed above. Du further teaches:
determining the directional cross component filter is enabled, if the flag is signaled in the encoded bit stream and has a first value (e.g. par. 216: describing that the JCF filter is enabled if the flag is signaled in the encoded bit stream is “on”, wherein the JCF filter is the equivalent of the directional cross component filter, and wherein the flag being “on” is the equivalent of the flag having a first value); and
determining the directional cross component filter is disabled, if the flag is signaled in the encoded bit stream and has a second value (e.g. par. 216: describing that the JCF filter is enabled if the flag is signaled in the encoded bit stream is “off”, wherein the JCF filter is the equivalent of the directional cross component filter, and wherein the flag being “off” is the equivalent of the flag having a second value).
Du does not explicitly teach:
determining the directional cross component filter is disabled, if the flag is not signaled in the encoded bit stream.
Hu, however, teaches a video decoding method and video decoding apparatus:
determining the directional cross component filter is disabled, if the flag is not signaled in the encoded bit stream (e.g. par. 168: describing that the system determines the cross component filter to be disabled if the flag is not signaled in the bitstream, wherein the cross component filter is the equivalent of the directional cross component filter).
It therefore would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to modify the teachings of Du by adding the teachings of Hu in order to determine the directional cross component filter is disable if the flag is not signaled in the encoded bit stream. One of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to make such a modification because the modification reduces processing time and increase coding efficiency (Hu, e.g. par. 7: describing the desire to reduce processing time and to increase coding efficiency).
Claim(s) 11 and 22 is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Du et al. (US 2021/0266604) (hereinafter Du) as applied to claims 10 and 21, respectively above, and further in view of Zhang et al. (US 2022/0264106) (hereinafter Zhang).
Regarding claims 11 and 22, Du teaches all of the limitations of claims 1, 8, and 10, and claims 12, 19, and 21, respectively, as discussed above. Du does not explicitly teach:
wherein the flag is signaled in a video frame header if: a constraint directional enhancement filter is enabled for a video sequence associated with the video frame header, and the video sequence comprises a chroma component.
Zhang, however, teaches a video decoding method and video decoding apparatus:
wherein the flag is signaled in a video frame header if: a constraint directional enhancement filter is enabled for a video sequence associated with the video frame header, and the video sequence comprises a chroma component (e.g. claim 1: describing that the system signals the cross component filter enabled flag if the associated loop filter is enabled for a video sequence, the video sequence including a chroma component, wherein the associated loop filter is the equivalent of the constraint directional enhancement filter).
It therefore would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to modify the teachings of Du by adding the teachings of Zhang in order to signal the flag if a constraint directional enhancement filter is enabled for a video sequence associated with the video frame header, and the video sequence comprises a chroma component. One of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to make such a modification because the modification improves coding efficiency.
Conclusion
